book.tiangongkaiwu.naili.name: Tiangong Kaiwu: On Grains (Naili)
book.tiangongkaiwu.naili.tooltip: Translate fragments at the Hanmo Tai to continue the unfinished text of this scroll.
book.tiangongkaiwu.naili.description: Naili comes first: the five grains are the very lifeblood of the people. From the General Discourse onward, entries on rice, wheat, millet, hemp and beans — and on rice lands, rice work, rice calamities and water works — unfold one by one. Translate fragments at the Hanmo Tai to continue the unfinished text of this scroll.
category.tiangongkaiwu.naili_juan.name: On Grains (Naili)
category.tiangongkaiwu.naili_juan.descri: The five grains are the very lifeblood of the people. From the General Discourse downward, rice takes the lead — rice lands, rice work, rice calamities and water works unfold in turn, while wheat and the lesser grains each claim their own entry. Translate the fragments, open the entries, and the whole living way of the five grains lies in this scroll.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_zonglun.name: General Discourse
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_zonglun.page1: Tiangong Kaiwu opens with the five grains. Master Song writes: the legend of Shennong is too faint to verify, yet the two words of his name — the Divine Husbandman — are on every tongue to this day. Man cannot live on air alone; it is the five grains that feed him. And the five grains cannot sow themselves; it is human labour that raises them. Grain and farmer complete each other; neither can be spared. Later generations of pampered sons, robed in silk and fed on meat, cannot tell one grain from another and forget where their dinners come from. These pages set down the ways of the field precisely so that no one forgets his roots.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_zonglun.page2: The five grains of the old books are hemp, beans, wheat, ji and shu — and conspicuously no rice. Not that the ancients thought little of it: the sages who wrote those books came from the northwest, where only dryland grains grew, so rice never entered their speech. Hemp is grown for its seed, beans need no introduction, wheat has its big and little kinds, ji is the non-sticky millet, shu the sticky yellow grain. Yet in our own day rice already supplies seven tenths of the nation's food — wet paddy and dry upland together fill the people's granaries.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_zonglun.page3: This scroll — Naili, On Grains — sets down the whole craft of the five grains, from seed to table. Beneath the General Discourse, rice takes the largest share: Rice Lands speaks of soil and manuring, Rice Work of ploughing, harrowing and transplanting, Rice Calamities of drought, flood and locusts, and Water Works of the noria and the well-sweep that raise water to the fields. Wheat, the millets, hemp and beans each have their own entry as well. Many of these chapters lie scattered among the folk as unreadable fragments. Place one in the Hanmo Tai with ink and paper ready, translate it sentence by sentence, and the chapter is unlocked. Take the finished fragment back and read it with a right-click — and a new page of the book will light up.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_do.name: Rice
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_do.page1: Rice comes in more varieties than any other grain, and the first thing to learn about a variety is stickiness. The non-glutinous plant is called jing; its husked grain, jingmi, cooks into firm, dry rice. The glutinous plant is called tu; its grain, nuomi, is sticky and made into wine and cakes. In the south no sticky millet is grown, so nearly all wine is brewed from glutinous rice.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_do.page2: Even within one kind the grain differs: awns long or short, kernels round or pointed, and names that change with local custom. Early and late varieties ripen weeks apart, so the farmer sows them in turn and keeps his fields green through the seasons.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_do.page3: Once the rice is in the field, the real work begins: which soil suits it, how it must be ploughed and harrowed, how flood, drought and insects are kept at bay, and how water is brought to it. These four matters are the subjects of the entries that follow — rice lands, rice work, rice calamities and water works.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_mai.name: Wheat
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_mai.page1: Wheat has fewer names than rice, but they are drawn clearly. Common wheat is called lai, chief of the wheats; barley is called mou, and also kuang. The oat and the buckwheat are the lesser kinds.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_mai.page2: Buckwheat loves cool weather and is sown in late summer and early autumn. Its stems redden, its seed is three-cornered, and it grinds into flour for noodles and cakes; when the land is worn and famine threatens, it is the easiest crop to bring in.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_mai.page3: Wheat likes high, dry ground and cannot abide standing water. Winter wheat must be sown before the first hard frost and is reaped in early summer. Then beans or millet take its place in the same field, year following year, so the land is never worn out — wheat and beans in turn, a practice as old as farming itself.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_mai.page4: A ripe wheat crop fears nothing so much as rain. As the ears turn yellow, the farmer watches for clear skies and starts the sickle. The cut sheaves are dried where they lie, then carted to the threshing floor. The grain is beaten out with the flail — a long handle with short sticks lashed to it, swung down so the kernels shower free — or, where oxen are to be had, a stone roller is dragged round the floor. The grain is winnowed of chaff, dried and stored. No sooner is the wheat in than the field must not lie idle: it is turned over at once, ready for the beans or millet to follow.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_mai.page5: Two things the wheat grower must guard against: wet ground and bitter cold. Where low fields hold water, the roots rot from long soaking; where autumn rains never cease, the sown seed lies in water and fails to sprout, the stand comes up thin, and the harvest is half lost before it begins. Hence wheat asks for high, dry land, with drains opened between the rows. Winter wheat must not be sown late either — after the first frosts the soil stiffens, roots cannot strike deep, and the next year's plants are weak and short-eared. Sow at the right depth and the right time, and the wheat will pass the winter in safety.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_dao_yi.name: Rice Lands
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_dao_yi.page1: Rice growing begins with the soil. A field cropped year after year without care turns sere and lifeless; the stalks may stand tall, but the grain is thin and sparse — the land's strength is not inexhaustible, it must be tended by man. The ancients called this "manuring": dung is no filthy thing, it is paying the land back what it is owed.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_dao_yi.page2: Manure is gathered from all quarters. Human and animal droppings come first, richest of all; next come the pressed cakes left from oil-making, of bean or rapeseed; wood ash, pared turf and rotted leaves each have their use as well. Near the hills one uses grass, near the town dung — whatever lies at hand; there is no fixed rule.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_dao_yi.page3: And the soil must be met on its own terms. Cold, sour paddy fields chill the young shoots, so at transplanting their roots are dipped in bone ash to give them warmth and a firm start. Sand, clay, sunny slope or shaded hollow — each wants its own feeding. Strength is kept by tending, and by tending well.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_dao_gong.name: Rice Work
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_dao_gong.page1: The rice harvest ends, but the field work does not. The farmer turns the soil at once, burying the stubble so the earth may mellow through the winter frosts — the "winter tilth" that gives next year its strength. Delay, and weed seeds take root, and come spring they will rob the rice of its food.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_dao_gong.page2: Field work follows a set order. The plough breaks the ground and opens the hard-pan; the harrow crumbles it, breaking the clods fine; the puddler levels it, smoothing the surface like a mirror, for only even water grows even seedlings. All three tasks lean on the ox — a stout beast is half a farmhouse's fortune.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_dao_gong.page3: A family without an ox can call on men instead: two shoulders under one plough-beam, pushing and pulling together, will turn a good patch in a day. And there is the nursery craft besides — a choice plot is set aside for seedlings, and one mu of nursery suffices to plant twenty-five mu of paddy. Raise first, then transplant: it saves seed and labour alike, and is the master key of rice farming.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_dao_zai.name: Rice Calamities
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_dao_zai.page1: Rice cannot do without water, yet it fears nothing more than losing it. In the weeks of flowering and grain-filling, let a paddy stand dry for ten days and the plants wither and die — "ten days without water, and the day of death is come." The rice farmer watches his water more keenly than he watches the sky.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_dao_zai.page2: The rice flower is small as millet-grain and opens before noon. If a gale blows while it blooms, the pollen scatters and the kernels come up empty. The nursery fears cold and wet above all: seed chilled in cold water, or soaked by weeks of cloud, rots in the mud before it can sprout — the ruin called "rotten seedlings." The cure lies in timing: steep the seed rightly, and let water in and out at the right hour.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_dao_zai.page3: Long drought breeds locusts. A swarm blots out the sun and strips every blade in an instant. The ancients had no remedy but their own hands: ditches dug to trap them, gongs beaten to drive them, ducks let loose to eat them — each kills a few, and every few counts. Against the locust year the farmhouse keeps its standing chores.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_shuili.name: Water Works
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_shuili.page1: All five grains lean on water, but rice most of all. A dryland crop makes do with a few rains; a paddy must be watered and drained again and again. When the field lies far from the stream, the ancients built machines to lift low water up to the high fields.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_shuili.page2: On swift rivers they set the noria: bamboo tubes bound about a wheel, turned by the current itself, dipping and lifting water to the bank without pause and without labour. On gentler streams the ox-wheel is used: the ox walks round his post and winds the paddles that carry the water over the dyke.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_shuili.page3: No river, no ox — still no hindrance. The tread-wheel lets several men tread the rungs together and raise the water; the hand-spun chain pump answers an emergency with one arm. At the well, a shallow one takes the sweep — a long pole balanced with a stone, pressing and springing — and a deep one the windlass. Machines differ in skill, but the principle is one: the machine is the water's stair, and water is the rice's life.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_shuji.name: The Millets
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_shuji.page1: Shu and ji were often confused by the ancients, yet they are two branches of one kind: the sticky one is shu, husked to yellow millet and fit for wine and cakes; the non-sticky one is ji, also called ji, cooked as plain grain. The "ji" among the five grains of the old books is this latter.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_shuji.page2: Liang and su form another pair. Su is the foxtail millet, its head like a dog's tail, its grain small and yellow, the daily food of the north. Liang is the choicer strain of su — larger and glossier of grain — counted a fine food in old times. The names are many, but the kinship runs through them all.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_shuji.page3: Shu, ji and su are dryland crops through and through: hardy against drought, undemanding of soil, sown on northern uplands in spring and reaped in autumn at the mercy of the sky — nothing like the rice that must drink every day. To live by the weather, to sow wide and reap thin, is the upland farmer's lot.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_ma.name: Hemp & Sesame
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_ma.page1: The "hemp" among the five grains is not the ramie of cloth-making but the cannabis plant. When the old books list the five grains as hemp, beans, wheat, ji and shu, it is the seed they mean: parched for eating, pressed for oil, one plant serving two ends. Seed for food — so it was in high antiquity.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_ma.page2: There is also the "barbarian hemp," the oily hemp, which we know today as sesame. Legend has it that Zhang Qian brought it back from Dayuan when he opened the western routes, hence the "barbarian" in its name. Its seeds are tiny and rich in oil; ground to paste, pressed for oil or sprinkled on cakes, it outdoes every grain in fragrance.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_ma.page3: Hemp is no staple in our day, yet it has never left the table: the oil is pressed from it, the sauces are seasoned with it, the fragrant seeds on the cake are it. Seed and oil alike, never wanting through the four seasons — hemp is the sixth grain beyond the five.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_shu.name: Beans
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_shu.page1: Shu is the common name for all the beans. Where the ancients said "shu," we say "bean": soybean, mung bean, pea, broad bean, azuki bean, cowpea — a host of kinds to match the rice. On the northern drylands the bean is the great crop of the field.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_shu.page2: No grain is eaten in more guises than the bean. Whole, it goes into the pot as bean rice; ground and set with brine it becomes tofu; pressed it yields oil; brewed it becomes sauce and fermented black beans; even its own sprouts are a vegetable. One bean can lay a whole table.
entry.tiangongkaiwu.naili_shu.page3: The bean's greatest worth is to the land. Its roots fix nitrogen and enrich the field; whatever is sown after beans grows strong. The ancients knew nothing of nitrogen, yet they long practised "manuring the field with mung beans" — bean feeds wheat and rice in endless rotation, and the land never tires.

block.tiangongkaiwu.tong_che.need_water: The wheel needs flowing water beneath it — build a weir to guide the current.
block.tiangongkaiwu.tong_che.plugged: Plugged with a wooden pin — the wheel stops.
block.tiangongkaiwu.tong_che.unplugged: Pin removed — the wheel turns again.
block.tiangongkaiwu.car.need_water: The chain pump must stand beside water (still water will do).
block.tiangongkaiwu.niu_che.how: Lead a leashed ox to the pump — it turns while the ox walks the wheel.
block.tiangongkaiwu.ta_che.how: Stand on the frame and treadle it.
block.tiangongkaiwu.ba_che.how: Stand beside it and crank it by hand.
block.tiangongkaiwu.dui.need_power: The pounder needs power — run a drive shaft beside it.
block.tiangongkaiwu.dui.need_container: Put a container (chest/hopper) above to hold grain; output drops into the container below, or pops out.
block.tiangongkaiwu.dui.power: Current power: %s (enough hulls it fine; too little yields only brown rice)
jei.tiangongkaiwu.pounding.input: Grain fed into the pounder (taken from the container above)
jei.tiangongkaiwu.pounding.result: Power ≥ %s: pounded through — yields white rice
jei.tiangongkaiwu.pounding.byproduct: The membrane pounded off becomes rice bran
jei.tiangongkaiwu.pounding.coarse: Not enough power (< %s): under-pounded — brown rice only
item.tiangongkaiwu.fen_fei.tip: Use on a paddy to ripen it (book: human and animal waste, many means to help it)
item.tiangongkaiwu.fen_fei.tip2: Source: feed rice bran to a pig, the pig returns manure. Works on any soil.
item.tiangongkaiwu.gu_hui.tip: Book: for soil that is cold and waterlogged, dip seedling roots in bone ash
item.tiangongkaiwu.gu_hui.tip2: Only for cold-slurry soil (clay paddies); not for warm sunny soil
item.tiangongkaiwu.shi_hui.tip: Book: lime steeped at the foot of the seedlings
item.tiangongkaiwu.shi_hui.tip2: Only for cold-slurry soil (clay paddies), like bone ash
item.tiangongkaiwu.rice_bran.fed: The pig has eaten the bran and returned a manure.
item.tiangongkaiwu.rice_bran.full: This one is already fed — come back in a moment.
block.tiangongkaiwu.fen_fei.used: Manure applied — the shoots leap up.
block.tiangongkaiwu.gu_hui.used: Bone ash at the roots — the cold paddy comes alive.
block.tiangongkaiwu.shi_hui.used: Lime steeped at the feet — the cold paddy comes alive.
block.tiangongkaiwu.shao_tu.used: Clods stacked, firewood pressed, the field burned — the tight soil loosens.
block.tiangongkaiwu.shao_tu.wrong: Not for loose soft soil — burning only helps gravel/coarse-dirt paddies (sneak + hold firewood).
block.tiangongkaiwu.hui.wrong: Not for warm sunny soil — bone ash and lime only work on cold-slurry (clay) paddies.
block.tiangongkaiwu.fertilize.dry: No water in the paddy — fertiliser would be wasted. Fetch water first.
block.tiangongkaiwu.fertilize.ripe: This one is already ripe; no need to spend fertiliser.
block.tiangongkaiwu.well.need_water: Must stand beside water — a shallow pool or small ditch will do.
block.tiangongkaiwu.jie_gao.how: A counterweighted beam lifts water by itself — but the yield is pitiful (book: jiegao and lulu, their toil is very slight indeed).
block.tiangongkaiwu.lu_lu.how: Someone must stand beside it to turn the crank — a bit faster than the shadoof, still far behind the water wheel.
block.tiangongkaiwu.feng_fan_che.how: The wind dies and it stops — this wheel only turns in rain. It REMOVES water, not draws it; useless for watering dry fields.
block.tiangongkaiwu.feng_fan_che.spinnin: Waiting on the wind — draining the marsh, one block at a time.
